# Kanazawa Notes

## Overview

Three nights in Kanazawa in October, arriving by rail from the east and leaving west toward the coast. The city escaped the wartime bombing and kept its old quarters, so the samurai streets and the teahouse lanes are the genuine article rather than a reconstruction. I came for those and for the seafood, and both delivered. The weather was mild and dry, the maples only starting to turn, and the light in the late afternoon was the best of the trip.

The 21st Century Museum is the modern counterweight, a low glass circle in the middle of a park, and I gave it a whole afternoon. The centre is compact and walkable, though the sights sit at the edges, so I used the buses and a day pass that paid for itself after three rides. I stayed in a small hotel near the station for 9000 yen a night, which put the markets a short walk away in the morning. The pace of the town is gentle and the crowds are thinner than in the big cities I had come from. The city is often skipped in favour of the bigger names, and I am glad I gave it the three nights. The station itself is worth ten minutes, with its wooden gate and glass dome, and the market sits just outside. I would come back in spring for the garden and use the city as a base for the coast.

## Food

The seafood here is the best I ate in the country, and that is a strong claim. Omicho market is the reason: a covered hall of stalls a few minutes from the station, open from morning, selling crab, uni, shrimp and every fish that comes off the sea of Japan. I ate a bowl of rice topped with raw shrimp and snow crab for 2800 yen and understood what the fuss was about. The stalls also grill scallops and skewers of tuna on the spot, two or three pieces for 600 yen.

Crab is the local luxury, and the full crabs in the windows cost a fortune, but a leg or two at a stall was within reach and enough to taste. Gold leaf turns up on everything, from sweets to sake to a whole soft-serve cone dusted with it, and I paid 900 yen for one mostly to say I had. The thin gold leaf has no taste, only the look. I ate a light dinner of sushi at a counter near the market for 2500 yen, and a bowl of local noodles for 1000 yen on the evening I was tired. A day trip to the coast brought me to a fishing village where a set lunch of grilled fish and rice cost 1500 yen. Eating at the market twice a day kept the bill reasonable for the quality. The rice here is a local variety and the sake too, and a small tasting flight at a brewery cost 1000 yen. I bought a box of gold-leaf sweets at the station on the way out and they lasted the train ride.

## Notes

The Nagamachi samurai district is a grid of narrow lanes with earthen walls and water channels running past the gates, and the entry to one of the old houses cost 550 yen and showed how the other half lived under the clan. The Higashi Chaya teahouse district is the other old quarter, wooden facades and lattice windows, and a teahouse tour there cost 750 yen with tea and a sweet. I walked both in the morning before the buses arrived. The garden near the castle is one of the three great ones and worth two hours, with its pines and its ponds. I took a bus to the coast on the last day and spent the afternoon on the shore. The bus to the coast runs a few times a day and the trip takes about an hour. The geisha houses in the east district are still working, and a few take visitors for tea in the afternoon; the one I chose was quiet and the garden behind it was the best small garden of the trip. Late in the day the lattice windows catch the low sun and the lanes empty, which is the time to walk them. The castle park is free and the gates are worth a look.
